text: A CIS Benchmark is a free, consensus-built hardening guide from the Center for Internet Security, worked out by a community of practitioners rather than written unilaterally by one vendor. A Benchmark exists for Ubuntu, RHEL, Debian, Docker, Kubernetes, and most other mainstream platforms, and every one of them is organized into numbered sections you can work through systematically instead of guessing at what 'secure' is supposed to mean on a given server.

Those sections read like a table of contents for everything that can go wrong on a default install: initial setup, services, network configuration, logging and auditing, access and authentication, and system maintenance. Every recommendation inside is also tagged Level 1 or Level 2 — Level 1 is a broad baseline with little functional impact; Level 2 is stricter defense-in-depth, reserved for environments like PCI-regulated systems where some functionality loss is acceptable.

A single recommendation, like disabling the cramfs filesystem, isn't just a sentence — it carries a rationale for why it matters, an audit command that reports the current state, a remediation procedure with the exact fix, and a mapping to the broader CIS Controls framework. Check first, then fix, then re-check: that structure is what makes a Benchmark something you automate against, not just read.

Nobody hand-applies a few hundred recommendations one at a time. A scanner like OpenSCAP or CIS-CAT runs the chosen profile against the host, producing a pass/fail report. The engineer triages the failures — some are real gaps, others are intentional exceptions, like a recommendation to disable IPv6 that would break a required application — remediates the real ones, and re-scans to confirm the compliance score actually improved.

A fresh install might score 60% against Level 1 Server; after remediation that can climb past 90%, with whatever's left documented as an accepted risk an auditor can review. That's the real deliverable: a number, and a paper trail behind every point still missing from 100. Next up: kernel hardening, tuning settings a filesystem-level benchmark check never touches.
